evidence: The card defines a Path as "a sequence of adjacent vertices with no repeated edge." That is the definition of a TRAIL/walk-with-no-repeated-edge, not a path. A path is a walk with NO REPEATED VERTICES (which automatically implies no repeated edge, but not conversely: a figure-eight-style trail can revisit a vertex while never reusing an edge, yet it is not a path). This is also internally inconsistent with the sibling ch11-cycle card, which defines a cycle as a "closed path with no repeated vertices except start/end" — that phrasing only makes sense if a plain path already forbids repeated vertices. The chapter's own proof-order item (ch11-p3) even writes "simple path," implying the unqualified card is meant to be the vertex-simple notion. The back is therefore factually incorrect for the term on the front.
proposedFix: Change back to: "A path is a sequence of adjacent vertices with no repeated vertex (equivalently, no repeated edge and no revisited vertex)." e.g. "A path is a walk $v_0,v_1,\dots,v_k$ of adjacent vertices with no repeated vertex."

evidence: The prompt asks which identity is correct for a nonnegative integer-valued X, and answerIndex=1 marks choice 1 ($E[X]=\sum_{t\ge1}P(X\ge t)$, the tail-sum formula) as the sole correct answer. But choice 0, $E[X]=\sum_{t\ge1}tP(X=t)$, is ALSO correct: the definition is $E[X]=\sum_{t\ge0}tP(X=t)$, and the omitted t=0 term is $0\cdot P(X=0)=0$, so $\sum_{t\ge1}tP(X=t)=\sum_{t\ge0}tP(X=t)=E[X]$. Two choices are simultaneously correct, violating MCQ uniqueness.

evidence: The back reads: 'A set is uncountable if no bijection with $\mathbb{N}$ exists.' This is false as a characterization of uncountable: every finite set also has no bijection with $\mathbb{N}$ (a bijection would force equal cardinality with an infinite set), yet finite sets are NOT uncountable. The correct notion is: uncountable = not countable, where countable means finite OR bijective with $\mathbb{N}$; equivalently uncountable means infinite AND no bijection with $\mathbb{N}$. As stated it wrongly classifies every finite set as uncountable, which genuinely misleads.
proposedFix: Change back to: 'A set is uncountable if it is infinite and cannot be put in bijection with $\mathbb{N}$ (equivalently, it is not countable).'
